WhoWeAre.title: Born from a friendship, a shared newsroom, and years of turning ideas into stories.
WhoWeAre.intro: We are Assia Touati and Imen Bliwa, two best friends who first met through work. What began as a professional relationship quickly became a friendship built around a shared passion for journalism, communication, language, and good storytelling.
WhoWeAre.imen: Imen is a journalist, translator and researcher working across Arabic, English and French, with more than a decade of experience in journalism, translation and international media. Her work has taken her across different subjects, audiences and formats, from journalistic reporting and research to translation and content development.
WhoWeAre.assia: Assia is an open-minded editor-in-chief with a strong editorial instinct and a talent for turning ideas into clear, engaging and meaningful content. Her experience in editorial work brings another essential perspective: understanding the audience, shaping the message and making content work as part of a larger product.
WhoWeAre.magazine: We first worked together at a magazine where we experienced something particularly valuable: building a successful media product from the inside.
WhoWeAre.learned: We learned how an idea becomes a story, how stories become a product, and how strong editorial work, communication and teamwork can create something people actually connect with.
WhoWeAre.meetings: We kept meeting at one of our favorite coffee places, at our offices, or simply whenever we had time to sit down and talk. We talked about our work, the media industry, businesses, communication, languages and all the things we thought could be done differently. And eventually, one idea kept coming back:

HowWeWork.title: From the first idea to the final story.
HowWeWork.standfirst: Good content doesn't start with a keyboard. It starts with listening, understanding, asking the right questions and knowing where to look.
HowWeWork.languageCardNote: Maghrebi Arabic nuance where it matters — not Gulf-standard MSA applied by default.
HowWeWork.tagline: Listen. Understand. Prepare. Go where the story is. Create. Translate. Edit. Deliver.
HowWeWork.closingNote: And when the next story comes, we're already there.

listen.title: We listen first
listen.body: Every assignment starts with a conversation. We want to understand what you need, who you are speaking to, what you want to achieve and what the story is really about.
listen.aside: We ask questions before we start producing. The better we understand the brief, the better we can tell the story.

approach.title: We build the right approach
approach.body: Not every story needs the same treatment. We bring together the right people, skills, languages and tools for each assignment.
list: Some require a journalist on the ground.
Some need translation that understands context, not just words.
approach.listLast: Others need all of it at once.

field.title: We go beyond the desk
field.body: Some stories cannot be told from behind a screen. When the assignment requires it, we are there — reporting, interviews, events, press coverage, research, fixing and multimedia content.
field.body2: Our experience in field journalism means we understand the realities of working on location: finding contacts, navigating the environment, arranging access and getting the material needed to tell the story properly.
field.aside: We don't just tell you what is happening. We go and find out.

purpose.title: We create with purpose
purpose.body: Whether we are writing an article, creating digital content, editing a text or producing communication material, we focus on clarity, accuracy, tone and audience.
purpose.aside: We don't believe in filling space. Every piece of content needs a reason to exist.

languages.title: We connect languages and cultures
languages.body: Translation, for us, is not simply replacing one word with another. We consider context, culture, tone, audience and purpose so the message feels natural in its new language while keeping the meaning and intention of the original.

deliver.title: We deliver
deliver.body: Content is often needed on time, not eventually. Once the work is agreed, we set the scope, timeline and deliverables clearly and keep communication open throughout the assignment.
deliver.body2: For urgent or field-based work, our experience allows us to respond quickly and work under pressure without losing sight of quality.
deliver.aside: We show up. We do the work. We deliver.

stay.title: And we stay involved
stay.body: For clients who need more than a one-off assignment, we can become an ongoing content and media partner — regular articles and translations, social content, editorial support, media coverage and field assignments on a recurring basis.
stay.aside: Because the best work often comes from knowing the client, understanding their voice and building trust over time.

FeaturedPost.standfirst: Most Arabic content aimed at North Africa is written for a Gulf ear. Your readers notice — even when they can't tell you why.
FeaturedPost.author: Imen Bliwa
FeaturedPost.caption: Caption line — where the photograph was taken and who took it.
FeaturedPost.b0: here is a version of Arabic that lives on brochures, in press releases and across half the region's websites. It is grammatically correct. It is also unmistakably borrowed — the register of a Gulf agency, applied to an audience in Tunis, Algiers or Casablanca that speaks and reads differently.
FeaturedPost.b1: Modern Standard Arabic is a real, shared language, and there are contexts where it is exactly right. The problem is not MSA itself. The problem is treating it as a neutral default, and assuming that a translator who has never worked with a North African audience will land the same way as one who has.
FeaturedPost.b3: Rarely the grammar. Almost always the vocabulary choices, the sentence rhythm, and the assumptions underneath: what needs explaining, what can be taken for granted, which institutions get named, which examples ring true. A Tunisian reader will finish the paragraph and come away with the impression that it was not written for them — without necessarily being able to point to the word that gave it away.
FeaturedPost.b4: Translation is not replacing one word with another. It is carrying context, culture, tone, audience and purpose across, so the message feels native in its new language.
FeaturedPost.b5: This is the part that no glossary and no machine solves for you. It is a judgement call made by someone who knows the audience, checked by an editor who also knows the audience — which is why we run every translation through both, in that order.
FeaturedPost.b6: Three questions before you commission anything in Arabic
b7: Where does the reader live, and what do they read on an ordinary day?
Is this a formal document, or is it meant to persuade someone?
Who is going to read the Arabic back before it publishes — and are they from the audience?
FeaturedPost.b8: If the answer to the third one is nobody, that is the gap. It is also the cheapest one to close.
FeaturedPost.bio: is a journalist, translator and researcher working across Arabic, English and French, and a co-founder of StoryBridge Content & Media.

PrivacyPage.title: Privacy Policy
PrivacyPage.standfirst: What we collect when you use this site, and what we do with it.
PrivacyPage.updated: Draft — 25 August 2026. Not yet reviewed by a lawyer; treat this as a description of practice, not a final legal document.

sections.heading: What we collect
body: If you send us a brief through the contact form, we store your name, email address, organisation, the kind of work you need, languages, deadline and the brief itself.
If you subscribe to The Bridge, our newsletter, we store your email address and nothing else — the signup form doesn't ask for a name.
We don't use tracking cookies, analytics scripts or advertising pixels on this site today. If that changes, this page will say so before it happens, not after.

sections.heading: Where it's stored
body: Everything above is stored in Google Cloud Firestore, in a database region located in the European Union. We chose that region for latency to our own base in Tunis and to keep content in the EU by default.
Only StoryBridge staff can read what you send us — a contact-form submission or a newsletter address is never public, and we don't sell or share it with anyone.

sections.heading: How we use it
body: A contact-form brief is used to reply to you about the work you're asking for. A newsletter subscription is used, once we start sending The Bridge, to send you that newsletter and nothing else — no other list, no resale.
We don't currently have an automated way to send you anything — that's genuinely still being built. Until it exists, subscribing saves your address; it doesn't put anything in your inbox.

sections.heading: How long we keep it
body: We haven't yet set a formal retention schedule. If you'd like something you sent us deleted, email hello@storybridge.news and we'll remove it.

sections.heading: Your rights
body: You can ask what we hold about you, ask us to correct it, or ask us to delete it, at any time, by emailing hello@storybridge.news. We aim to handle these in the spirit of the EU's GDPR, though we haven't formally certified compliance with it.

CookiePage.title: Cookie Policy
CookiePage.standfirst: The short version: this site still doesn't set any cookies — not even for analytics.

sections.heading: What we use today
body: This site uses Plausible, a privacy-first analytics tool, to see how many people visit and which pages they read — in aggregate, never as individuals. Plausible doesn't use cookies, doesn't collect personal data, and can't track you across other websites. Language (English, French or Arabic) is chosen by the URL you're on, not stored in a cookie either.

The one place cookies genuinely are used is our staff CMS, a separate, sign-in-only tool at a different address — Firebase Authentication sets a session cookie there so a signed-in staff member stays signed in. That has nothing to do with visitors to this site.

sections.heading: Why we still show a notice
body: Plausible's cookie-free design means the law doesn't require asking your permission before it runs — but we'd rather tell you it's there than rely on that technicality. The small notice on your first visit is exactly that: a heads-up, not a gate.
